title: Utilise quality assessment principles for the classification of perishable produce

lessons.title: Why produce is classified, and packing and marking first
lessons.html:
The rationale for classification

Classification means sorting produce into classes according to quality. It gives buyers and sellers a common language. A buyer in London who orders Class 1 navels knows what to expect without seeing the fruit. Classification also:

  • protects consumers from receiving produce that is not as described;
  • allows fair pricing, with higher prices for higher classes;
  • protects the reputation of South African produce in export markets;
  • lets growers sell lower classes in suitable markets instead of wasting them, for example Class 2 to other markets or the local market, and lower grades to processors.

Influences on how classes are determined

Classes are set in the export standards under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 and are influenced by:

  • international standards and the requirements of importing countries;
  • what consumers and retailers in the markets expect;
  • what the industry can realistically produce;
  • food safety and phytosanitary considerations.

Packaging and marking before classing

Before a consignment can be classed and inspected, it must comply with the prescribed packing and marking requirements:

  • Packaging: approved container types, strong enough for stacking and humidity, clean, with ventilation, and the correct inner packaging.
  • Packing: fruit packed firmly and uniformly, with the correct count or mass, and no mixing of classes or sizes unless allowed.
  • Marking: each carton clearly marked with the product, cultivar, class, count or size, the packer or exporter identification, the production unit code and packhouse code, and other details the standards require.
  • Uniformity: all cartons in a consignment of one class must look the same and carry the same markings.

If marking or packing is wrong, the consignment can fail even if the fruit inside meets the class. A carton marked Class 1 must contain Class 1 fruit; anything else is misrepresentation.

lessons.title: Physiological parameters and senescence
lessons.html:
Physiological parameters used in classification

Classification looks at the external and internal condition of produce. The main parameters are:

  • Maturity: whether the fruit has reached the stage needed to ripen or eat well, measured by indicators such as firmness, total soluble solids (TSS), acid, starch, juice content, dry matter or colour depending on the product.
  • Size and mass: measured against the declared count or size range.
  • Colour: skin and ground colour compared with standard colour charts.
  • Shape: typical of the cultivar.
  • Firmness and turgidity: fruit should be firm and not shrivelled.
  • Freedom from defects: blemishes, bruises, wounds, pest damage and decay.
  • Physiological disorders: such as bitter pit, chilling injury, internal browning or creasing.

Senescence and what speeds it up

Senescence is the final stage of the produce's life, when tissues break down and quality is lost. Fruit that is entering senescence softens, loses colour and flavour, shrivels and becomes more prone to decay. Factors that bring on senescence sooner include:

  • High temperature: the main factor. Every hour at warm temperatures uses up storage life.
  • Ethylene: speeds ripening and ageing, especially in climacteric fruit.
  • Water loss: low humidity and air movement cause shrivel.
  • Mechanical damage: bruises and wounds increase respiration and invite decay.
  • Over-maturity at harvest: fruit picked late has less storage life.
  • Long storage: time itself.

Effect on classification

As senescence progresses, fruit that was Class 1 at packing can fall below class requirements: it may become too soft, discoloured or shrivelled, or develop decay and disorders. That is why inspectors look at condition as well as quality, and why fruit must be classed and shipped promptly, under a proper cold chain.

lessons.title: Criteria for determining the class
lessons.html:
How the class is decided

The export standards set criteria for each class. While details differ per product, the principles are the same:

ClassGeneral description
Class 1Good quality, typical of the cultivar, with only slight defects within strict tolerances; for the main export markets
Class 2Marketable quality with more defects allowed, provided keeping quality and appearance are maintained
Lower gradesFruit not meeting export classes, for local market or processing as the rules allow

Applying the criteria

  1. Draw a representative sample at random from the consignment, as prescribed.
  2. Check minimum requirements that apply to all classes: sound, clean, free from pests and abnormal moisture, and mature enough.
  3. Measure maturity indices and compare with minimums.
  4. Check size and count against the marking.
  5. Score defects: count each defective fruit by defect type and severity.
  6. Calculate percentages of defects in the sample.
  7. Compare with tolerances for the declared class. Serious defects such as decay have lower tolerances than minor cosmetic marks.
  8. Decide: the consignment meets the declared class, must be downgraded, or is rejected.

Example

A sample of 200 pears declared as Class 1 contains 6 fruit with friction marks larger than allowed for Class 1 and 1 fruit with decay. The assessor calculates 3 percent friction marks and 0.5 percent decay and compares each with the Class 1 tolerances for pears. If either exceeds its tolerance, the consignment cannot pass as Class 1.

Assessors must be objective, use calibrated instruments, follow the standard exactly and record their results. Personal opinions about what looks good enough have no place in classification.

Key points

  • Classification gives buyers and sellers a common language and fair pricing.
  • Packing and marking must comply before a consignment can be classed.
  • Maturity, size, colour, shape, defects and disorders are assessed.
  • Heat, ethylene, water loss, damage and over-maturity speed senescence.
  • Defect percentages are compared with the tolerances for the declared class.
